description: Somos un equipo miembros de JEO (Jovenes En Orbita), nos unimos para resolver y participar de una solución que ayude a la comunidad y al ecosistema espacial. También buscamos combinar nuestras habilidades, ideas y creatividad para desarrollar soluciones innovadoras.
summary:
HexAstra is a platform designed to connect extraterrestrial environments with potential Earth analogues using open data. Preparing missions to the Moon or Mars involves complex decisions, including identifying suitable locations to test technologies on Earth.
Our solution introduces TASI, a five-dimensional index that compares geological characteristics, topography, climate, available resources, and operational conditions. It helps teams narrow their search, prioritize resources, and understand the similarities between different environments.
Through an interactive platform, users can select a planetary destination, such as Arsia Mons on Mars, and search for comparable locations worldwide. In easy mode, the system automatically identifies promising candidates, while advanced mode allows users to customize the importance of each comparison dimension.
HexAstra also provides interactive map layers, including satellite imagery, elevation, vegetation, snow, and ground temperature. Every metric is linked to its data source, and missing information is clearly identified.
The platform combines open datasets from NASA and Earth observation sources. TASI only calculates scores using available data and is presented as a proposed index, not an official scientific standard.
Although Earth cannot reproduce conditions such as extraterrestrial gravity, vacuum, or radiation, HexAstra provides a starting point for identifying and evaluating potential analogue sites.
details:
HexAstra is an interactive web platform that helps users identify and understand terrestrial environments that may serve as analogs for exploration sites on the Moon and Mars. It connects open scientific data with an accessible visual experience, allowing users to compare locations, investigate their similarities, and understand the limits of each analogy.

Preparing a space mission involves complex decisions about where and how to test instruments, robots, scientific methods, and operational procedures. Terrestrial analog environments provide opportunities to perform some of these tests before a mission reaches another planetary body. However, choosing a useful analog requires more than finding a landscape that looks similar. A volcanic field may resemble a Martian site geologically while experiencing very different temperatures. A polar environment may offer relevant conditions for studying ice while presenting different terrain or logistical constraints.

HexAstra addresses this challenge by organizing comparisons around evidence, purpose, and transparency. Our current prototype connects 60 terrestrial sites with 14 destinations on the Moon and Mars. The catalog includes volcanic landscapes, deserts, salt flats, impact structures, polar environments, and lava-related features. It combines well-known analog environments with less-studied candidates, with particular attention to locations in Argentina.

Places such as Campo de Piedra Pómez, Payún Matrú, and Laguna de Antofagasta illustrate the opportunity to examine environments beyond the most frequently referenced analog sites. Their inclusion provides a starting point for further investigation, supported by documented measurements and published references.

The user experience begins with an interactive three-dimensional Earth. A guided workflow helps users define a comparison in three steps: select the Moon or Mars, choose a specific destination, and select a mission focus. Users can prioritize a balanced comparison, terrain similarity, extreme environmental conditions, or characteristics relevant to robotic testing. They can also search worldwide or narrow the candidate catalog by continent and country.

When a mission is launched, the globe moves toward the highest-ranked comparable terrestrial candidate and opens its comparison. The strongest positive matches receive a visual pulse, helping users recognize where to begin exploring. Selecting another point reveals its corresponding measurements, score, similarities, differences, and sources. This interaction turns a catalog of locations into a practical sequence of questions: Why does this place resemble the destination? Which characteristics support the comparison? Where does the analogy break down? What evidence is still missing?

We designed TASI, the Terrestrial Analog Similarity Index, to structure these comparisons. TASI is our team’s proposed index, built using established comparison methods and documented scientific inputs. The framework organizes evidence into five dimensions:

  • Geology and materials: geological composition categories, rock families, and impact origin where comparable information is available.
  • Terrain and topography: relative relief, slope, and surface roughness.
  • Thermal environment and illumination: temperature, daily temperature variation, and illumination metrics where supported by the data.
  • Volatiles, water, and ice: precipitation and relevant ice indicators, with their definitions and limitations preserved.
  • Operational conditions: information relevant to testing and field campaigns, including documented terrestrial access and logistical context.

The importance of these dimensions depends on the intended test. A team investigating rover mobility may prioritize terrain differently from a team studying thermal conditions or geological processes. HexAstra makes those priorities explicit through mission presets and adjustable weights.

TASI combines the component similarities supported by comparable evidence on both sides of a pair. The weights are renormalized over the available components, and the application reports how much evidence supports the result. A missing value remains missing rather than becoming an invented measurement or an artificial zero.

Terrain comparison uses Mahalanobis distance over relative relief, slope, and roughness. This method accounts for relationships among those variables, rather than treating every difference as independent. Geological comparison uses sourced map categories and reports the available composition and impact-origin evidence. Environmental comparisons use shared metrics with documented scaling. The result is presented on a scale from zero to one hundred, accompanied by a breakdown and an explanation.

Coverage is essential to interpreting that number. A score based on two available dimensions conveys different information from a score supported by four. The application keeps evidence coverage visible so users can assess both the apparent similarity and the completeness of the comparison. TASI represents similarity under the selected inputs and priorities; it does not establish that a location is suitable for a real mission.

A demonstration compares Arsia Mons on Mars with Laguna de Antofagasta in Argentina. With the terrain-focused preset and the search restricted to Argentina, Laguna de Antofagasta is the highest-ranked comparable candidate, with a displayed TASI score of 72.7. The comparison identifies a strong match in the available geological categories while showing a substantial difference in thermal conditions. Increasing the terrain weight changes the displayed score to 70.9 for the same pair. This example makes the effect of user priorities visible and shows why a single score should be read alongside its component evidence.

For deeper investigation, HexAstra includes an advanced interface with Earth and planetary maps displayed side by side. Users can adjust dimension weights, change filters, inspect measurements, and explore map layers. Earth layers include satellite imagery, OpenStreetMap, NASA GIBS MODIS imagery, and land-surface temperature visualization. Each layer supports a different type of inspection, such as examining landscape patterns, access routes, vegetation, snow, or surface thermal conditions. The interface distinguishes the visual context provided by a map layer from the numerical measurements used in the comparison.

Open data are central to the project. The scientific workflow incorporates documented planetary and terrestrial sources, including lunar LOLA and Martian MOLA-related terrain products, Diviner temperature information, geological maps, terrestrial elevation data, and climate data. Other resources, including Natural Earth and OpenStreetMap, support geographic organization and contextual information.

Measurements retain their provenance, units, quality, and relevant interpretation notes. Where appropriate, the project distinguishes measured, modeled, derived, and convention-based values. This matters because a modeled climate value, a published temperature range, and a direct instrument measurement carry different meanings. Preserving those distinctions helps users understand what a comparison can support.

We also considered differences in spatial resolution and physical definition. Data products may describe different sampling areas or native resolutions. Surface temperature and near-surface air temperature are different quantities. A geological map category provides different evidence from a measured mineral spectrum. An indicator of ice stability does not automatically establish the presence of detected ice. These distinctions inform the project’s data handling and its explanations.

The frontend was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Three.js powers the immersive Earth and textured planetary visuals, while Leaflet supports the two-dimensional Earth and planetary maps. The interface supports English and Spanish, selects an initial language from the browser, and allows users to save a manual preference. We considered responsive layouts, keyboard access, visible focus, readable contrast, and reduced-motion preferences when designing the experience.

The reference scientific backend was developed in Python, using FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, and supporting geospatial tools. The development architecture includes PostgreSQL with PostGIS for organizing geographic information and sourced measurements. Separate Earth and planetary services provide catalogs, feature vectors, comparison methods, rankings, and supporting information.

The public demonstration runs on Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions. A versioned export of verified evidence supports a JavaScript runtime that filters candidates and calculates adjusted rankings. This deployment allows the demonstration to remain accessible without depending on a team member’s computer, a local database, or a temporary tunnel. The published catalog is a documented release that can be refreshed after scientific data updates are reviewed.

We used Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration. Validation included Python tests, JavaScript tests, and browser-based checks with Playwright. The hosted ranking implementation was compared with the Python reference across 60 scenarios covering all 14 destinations, different presets, regional filters, masking, adjustable terrain sensitivity, zero weights, and missing components. AI assistants supported development, interface iteration, documentation, and demonstration preparation; their use is documented alongside external resources.

HexAstra’s creativity lies in bringing these elements into one understandable workflow. It connects planetary destinations, terrestrial candidates, adjustable priorities, dimensional explanations, and source-level evidence in a single visual experience. The interaction helps users explore a scientific question while retaining access to the information needed to question the result. Its focus on Argentine environments also creates an opportunity to connect local landscapes and institutions with broader planetary exploration research.

The intended benefits include helping researchers, robotics teams, universities, educators, and field-campaign planners narrow an initial search, compare alternatives, identify evidence gaps, and focus subsequent investigation. The project may support more deliberate use of time and resources by helping teams decide where to look first. Demonstrating actual cost reductions or improved mission outcomes would require further validation with real users and field campaigns.

The educational impact is also important. HexAstra makes an abstract idea tangible: an Earth location can resemble another world in one characteristic and differ strongly in another. Users can see how changing priorities affects a result, how missing evidence changes its interpretation, and how open scientific data become part of a reasoned comparison.

Throughout development, we considered the physical limits of terrestrial analogs. Earth does not reproduce lunar or Martian gravity, the lunar vacuum, the thin Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environments of those bodies. We therefore distinguish similarity from mission suitability and retain physical context alongside the comparison. Further work includes expanding the evidence base, improving comparable measurements, developing approaches to identify additional candidates beyond the curated catalog, and validating promising analogies through expert review and field investigation.

Our intended impact is to make the first stages of analog-site exploration more accessible, systematic, and transparent. HexAstra gives experts and learners an evidence-based starting point: where to look, what may be comparable, what differs, and what should be investigated next.
